newsitem.title: BOSNIA: SOCCER-ITALY'S STARS COME TO TERMS WITH SARAJEVO.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALY'S STARS COME TO TERMS WITH SARAJEVO.

text.p: Italy striker Fabrizio Ravanelli and his multi-millionaire team mates on Tuesday came face to face with the harsh reality of once-besieged Sarajevo.

"What's your name?" five-year-old Amir asked the silver- haired Middlesbrough player, a question few children in England or Italy would need to ask, as he visited a city hospital with the squad and officials.
"Fabrizio," whispered Ravanelli, as he gently stroked the hand of a badly burned child in the Kosevo hospital.
Kosevo hospital was where many of the 10,000 Sarajevo citizens who died or the 50,000 who were injured during the siege were brought. The siege lasted for most of the 43-month-long war in Bosnia.
Fellow-attacker Gianfranco Zola produced faint smiles as he tried to convince Amir that his photograph was more worth having than that of his team mates.
"He's ugly, forget him. And him," he said of defender Moreno Torricelli and goalkeeper Francesco Toldo.

From the moment the Italian team arrived at Sarajevo's bomb-damaged airport for Wednesday's historic friendly against Bosnia at the Kosevo stadium, the symbolism and intent to bring Italian goodwill to the Bosnian capital was evident.
The match will be Bosnia's first home game as an independent country and the first international in the restored stadium, near the former front line, since before the war.
Captain Paolo Maldini posed with airport staff in the arrivals hall in front of a poster marking 20 years since the death of French poet Andre Malraux.
"I have learned that a life is worth nothing but that nothing is worth a life," the words on it read.
Leaving the airport by bus, the team was driven past the shattered and burnt-out apartment blocks that surround the airport and once marked the front line.

"I had only ever seen Sarajevo on television but what you see when you arrive is so different," striker Pierluigi Casiraghi told Reuters. "It's a city that is trying to rebuild itself but which has suffered so much.
"And it's only one hour away from Italy. Maybe the thing that struck me most was the feeling of impotence."
Ravanelli was equally humbled.
"You only have to arrive at the airport and see everything that has happened ... We are very lucky," he said.
"I think soccer is something very important and that it can really do something exceptional for peace."
That message was reiterated later by Italian and Bosnian soccer officials, who exchanged mementoes.
Italian soccer commissioner Raffaele Pagnozzi read out at a news conference a letter from deputy Italian prime minister Walter Veltroni, who had been due to attend the match.

"The game between Bosnia and Italy goes far beyond a sporting event and takes on a very high human and social significance, helping to restore the climate of peace in this battered land," Veltroni wrote.
For some, the miracle had already happened.
"If someone had told me two years ago that I would be standing here with Paolo Maldini, I would never have believed them," commented one observer at the hospital.
